q: Which molecule crosses a phospholipid bilayer most easily by simple diffusion?
e: Small, nonpolar molecules like O₂ and CO₂ pass straight through the hydrophobic core. Ions and large polar molecules need channels or carriers.

q: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves ions in which way for each ATP it uses?
a: 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell
w: 2 Na⁺ out of the cell and 3 K⁺ into the cell
3 Na⁺ into the cell and 2 K⁺ out of the cell
3 K⁺ out of the cell and 2 Na⁺ into the cell
e: This is primary active transport. Because it moves net positive charge out, it also contributes slightly to the negative resting membrane potential.

q: The SGLT transporter brings glucose into intestinal cells against its gradient by coupling it to Na⁺ moving down its gradient. This is:
e: The transporter uses no ATP itself. It relies on the Na⁺ gradient that the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase builds with ATP.

q: Adding cholesterol to a membrane at body temperature generally:
a: Reduces fluidity by restricting phospholipid movement
w: Greatly increases fluidity by spreading phospholipids apart
Makes the membrane far more permeable to small ions
Has no effect, because cholesterol stays outside the bilayer
e: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer: it stiffens membranes at high temperature and prevents tight packing at low temperature.

q: Phospholipids with unsaturated fatty acid tails make membranes:
a: More fluid, because the cis double bonds create kinks that prevent tight packing
w: Less fluid, because double bonds hold neighboring tails more tightly together
More rigid, because the straight tails can line up and pack closely together
Impermeable to water, because double bonds repel the polar water molecules
e: Kinked tails can't line up closely, so the membrane stays fluid at lower temperatures.

q: Proteins destined for secretion are made on ribosomes attached to the:
e: A signal sequence directs the ribosome to the rough ER. Proteins then move to the Golgi for modification and packaging into vesicles.

q: Which organelle detoxifies drugs in liver cells and makes steroids in gland cells?
e: The smooth ER handles lipid synthesis, detoxification and calcium storage. It has no ribosomes.

q: Peroxisomes are best known for:
a: Breaking down very long-chain fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide
w: Synthesizing and assembling ribosomal RNA subunits
Sorting and packaging proteins into secretory vesicles
Producing most of the cell's ATP by oxidative phosphorylation
e: Peroxisomes run oxidation reactions that make H₂O₂, then use catalase to break it down.

q: Lysosomal enzymes work best at about pH 5. What is the advantage of this?
a: Enzymes that leak into the neutral cytosol are much less active
w: The enzymes stay equally active anywhere they end up in the cell
The acidic interior lets the lysosome make its own ATP from protons
Low pH stops the enzymes from being made in the rough ER by mistake
e: Acid hydrolases are largely inactive at the cytosol's pH of about 7.2, which protects the cell from digesting itself.

q: Which cytoskeletal element forms the mitotic spindle and the core of cilia and flagella?
e: Microtubules are tubulin polymers. Eukaryotic cilia and flagella use a 9 + 2 arrangement driven by dynein.

q: Which cell junction prevents fluid from leaking between epithelial cells?
e: Tight junctions seal neighboring cells together. Gap junctions let small molecules pass between cells, and desmosomes anchor cells mechanically.

q: Which of these is a connective tissue?
e: Connective tissues, including blood, bone, cartilage and adipose tissue, are cells surrounded by extracellular matrix. Epidermis and gut lining are epithelia.

q: Which feature do prokaryotic cells have that eukaryotic cells lack?
e: Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes (30S + 50S). Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, which is why some antibiotics can target bacteria selectively.

q: Gram-positive bacteria stain purple in a Gram stain because they have:
a: A thick peptidoglycan cell wall that holds the crystal violet dye
w: An outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide that traps the dye
No cell wall at all, so the dye stains the membrane directly
A thin peptidoglycan layer sandwiched between two cell membranes
e: Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane. They lose the dye and stain pink with the counterstain.

q: Transfer of a plasmid between bacteria through a sex pilus is called:
e: Transformation is taking up free DNA from the environment. Transduction is DNA transfer carried by a bacteriophage.

q: Bacteria reproduce asexually by:
e: The circular chromosome is copied and the cell divides in two. It's faster than mitosis and has no spindle.

q: A retrovirus like HIV inserts its genes into the host genome by:
a: Using reverse transcriptase to copy its RNA into DNA, then integrase to insert it
w: Inserting its single-stranded RNA genome directly into a host chromosome
Having host ribosomes translate its RNA genome into a matching DNA copy
Using host RNA polymerase II to copy its RNA genome into double-stranded DNA
e: Reverse transcription makes a DNA copy, and integrase splices it into host DNA as a provirus.

q: In the lysogenic cycle, a bacteriophage:
a: Integrates its genome into the host chromosome and is copied with it
w: Immediately makes new phages and then bursts the host cell open
Degrades the host chromosome and reuses its nucleotides for copies
Stays outside the cell, attached to the cell wall, until conditions change
e: The integrated prophage is passed to daughter cells. Stress can later trigger it to enter the lytic cycle.

q: Which statement about viruses is true?
a: They need a host cell's machinery to replicate
w: They make ATP through their own metabolism
They all contain both DNA and RNA
e: Viruses have DNA or RNA (not both) in a protein coat, have no metabolism, and replicate only inside host cells.

q: DNA replication occurs during which phase of the cell cycle?
e: Interphase is G₁ (growth), S (DNA synthesis) and G₂ (preparation for mitosis).

q: During which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles?
e: In anaphase, cohesin is cleaved and kinetochore microtubules shorten, pulling chromatids apart.

q: The tumor suppressor p53 helps prevent cancer mainly by:
a: Halting the cell cycle or triggering apoptosis when DNA is damaged
w: Pushing cells with damaged DNA past the G₁ checkpoint into S phase
Lengthening telomeres so damaged chromosomes stay stable after division
Speeding up mitosis so that cells with damaged DNA are diluted out
e: p53 is mutated in many cancers. Without it, damaged cells keep dividing.

q: Proto-oncogenes become oncogenes through mutations that typically:
a: Increase their activity, promoting uncontrolled division
w: Destroy their function, the way tumor suppressors are lost
Silence them completely so that division can't be controlled
Make them recessive, so both copies must be mutated first
e: Oncogene mutations are usually gain-of-function and dominant: one mutated copy can push division. Tumor suppressors usually need both copies lost.

q: The three germ layers form during which stage of embryonic development?
e: Gastrulation turns the blastula into a gastrula with ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.

q: Which germ layer gives rise to the nervous system and the epidermis?
e: Ectoderm forms the nervous system and skin epidermis. Mesoderm forms muscle, bone, blood and kidneys. Endoderm lines the gut and forms the lungs, liver and pancreas.

q: Which germ layer gives rise to the heart, skeletal muscle and kidneys?
e: Mesoderm is the middle layer and forms most muscle, the circulatory system, bones and the urogenital system.

q: Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that apoptosis:
a: Is an orderly, programmed process that does not trigger inflammation
w: Causes cells to swell, burst and release their contents into the tissue
Only happens after a physical injury or a sudden loss of blood flow
Triggers a strong inflammatory response that recruits immune cells nearby
e: Apoptotic cells shrink and break into membrane-bound blebs that are quietly engulfed. Necrotic cells burst and release contents that cause inflammation.

q: Embryonic stem cells from the inner cell mass are described as:
a: Pluripotent: they can become any cell of the body but not the placenta
w: Totipotent: they can become any cell of the body including the placenta
Unipotent: they can become only one cell type, like a skin precursor
Multipotent: they can become cells of only one tissue family, like blood
e: Only the zygote and very early blastomeres are totipotent. Adult stem cells, like blood stem cells, are usually multipotent.

q: The depolarization phase of a neuron's action potential is caused by:
a: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels opening and Na⁺ rushing in
w: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels opening and K⁺ rushing out
e: Na⁺ influx drives the membrane toward +30 mV or so. Repolarization follows as Na⁺ channels inactivate and K⁺ channels open.

q: The absolute refractory period exists mainly because:
a: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen yet
w: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels have all closed and cannot reopen
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump stops working until the gradient recovers
The axon terminal has run out of neurotransmitter vesicles
e: No stimulus, however strong, can fire another action potential until Na⁺ channels recover from inactivation. This also makes signals travel one way.

q: Myelin speeds up action potential conduction by:
a: Insulating the axon so the signal jumps between nodes of Ranvier
w: Adding many more Na⁺ channels along the entire length of the axon
Narrowing the axon so that current flows through it much faster
Releasing neurotransmitter at each node of Ranvier to relay the signal
e: This is saltatory conduction. Schwann cells make myelin in the peripheral nervous system, and oligodendrocytes make it in the CNS.

q: Arrival of an action potential at the axon terminal triggers neurotransmitter release by opening:
e: Ca²⁺ influx causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release their contents by exocytosis.

q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the vertebrate neuromuscular junction?
e: Acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptors on skeletal muscle. Acetylcholinesterase quickly breaks it down to end the signal.

q: Which division of the autonomic nervous system increases heart rate and dilates the pupils?
e: Sympathetic is fight-or-flight. Parasympathetic is rest-and-digest: it slows the heart, constricts pupils and promotes digestion.

q: In a simple knee-jerk reflex, the sensory neuron synapses directly with:
a: A motor neuron in the spinal cord
w: A neuron in the cerebral cortex
e: The patellar reflex is monosynaptic: the signal goes from muscle spindle to spinal cord to motor neuron, without involving the brain.

q: Steroid hormones such as cortisol act on target cells mainly by:
a: Crossing the membrane and binding intracellular receptors that alter transcription
w: Binding receptors on the cell surface that activate adenylyl cyclase and cAMP
Binding ligand-gated ion channels that directly depolarize the cell membrane
Being taken in by endocytosis and broken down to release their amino acids
e: Steroids are lipid-soluble. Their effects are slower but longer lasting than those of peptide hormones, which use surface receptors and second messengers.

q: Which hormone is released by the posterior pituitary?
e: The posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin, which are made in the hypothalamus. The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones, including GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin.

q: High levels of thyroid hormone in the blood reduce TSH secretion. This is an example of:
e: T₃ and T₄ inhibit TRH release from the hypothalamus and TSH release from the anterior pituitary, keeping levels steady.

q: Which hormone lowers blood calcium?
e: Calcitonin from the thyroid's C cells inhibits osteoclasts. Parathyroid hormone and calcitriol raise blood calcium.

q: The adrenal medulla secretes:
e: The medulla acts as part of the sympathetic nervous system. The adrenal cortex makes steroids such as cortisol and aldosterone.

q: Oxygenated blood returning from the lungs enters which chamber of the heart first?
e: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood to the left atrium. It then passes to the left ventricle and out the aorta.

q: Where is the heart's normal pacemaker located?
e: The SA node in the right atrium fires fastest and sets the rhythm. The AV node delays the signal so the atria finish contracting before the ventricles do.

q: Cardiac output equals:
e: At rest, about 70 beats/min × 70 mL/beat ≈ 5 L/min.

q: Which type of blood vessel has the greatest total cross-sectional area?
e: Capillaries are individually tiny, but there are billions. Their huge combined area means blood moves slowest there, giving time for exchange.

q: Gas exchange in the lungs takes place across the walls of the:
e: Alveoli have thin walls surrounded by capillaries. The airways before them form the conducting zone.

q: Surfactant in the alveoli helps breathing by:
a: Lowering surface tension so alveoli don't collapse
w: Raising surface tension to keep alveoli open
Transporting O₂ across the alveolar wall
e: Premature babies may lack enough surfactant, which leads to respiratory distress syndrome.

q: Most CO₂ is carried in the blood as:
w: CO₂ bound to the heme iron of hemoglobin
e: About 70% travels as bicarbonate after carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells converts it. Some binds to globin as carbamino groups, not to the iron.

q: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and:
a: Chest volume increases, so pressure in the lungs drops below atmospheric pressure
w: Chest volume decreases, so pressure in the lungs rises and air is pushed out
Chest volume increases, so pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric
The pleural space fills with air, which pulls the lungs outward to inflate
e: By Boyle's law, larger volume means lower pressure, so air flows in. Quiet expiration is mostly passive recoil.

q: Most reabsorption of filtered water, glucose and amino acids happens in the:
e: The PCT reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered Na⁺ and water and nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids.

q: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water reabsorption by:
a: Inserting aquaporins into the collecting duct
w: Blocking aquaporins in the loop of Henle
e: ADH lets the collecting duct absorb more water from the urine, which concentrates the urine and reduces water loss.

q: Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron to:
a: Increase Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion
w: Decrease Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion
e: Water follows the reabsorbed sodium, which raises blood volume and blood pressure. Aldosterone release is triggered by angiotensin II and high blood K⁺.

q: The loop of Henle's main job is to:
a: Build a salt gradient in the medulla so urine can be concentrated
w: Filter blood plasma into Bowman's capsule under high pressure
Secrete renin into the blood when kidney blood pressure falls
Reabsorb nearly all of the filtered glucose and amino acids
e: The descending limb lets water out, and the ascending limb pumps salt out without water. Together they form a countercurrent multiplier.

q: Which enzyme begins starch digestion in the mouth?
e: Amylase breaks starch into smaller sugars. Pepsin starts protein digestion in the stomach, and pancreatic enzymes finish most digestion in the small intestine.

q: Bile helps digest fats by:
a: Emulsifying fat into small droplets so lipase can reach more of it
w: Hydrolyzing triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol
Breaking peptide bonds between amino acids in dietary protein
Neutralizing stomach acid with large amounts of bicarbonate ions
e: Bile salts are amphipathic detergents. Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gallbladder, and it contains no digestive enzymes.

q: Which hormone is released when acidic chyme enters the duodenum and stimulates the pancreas to secrete bicarbonate?
e: Secretin raises pancreatic HCO₃⁻ to neutralize acid. CCK responds to fats and proteins by triggering enzyme release and gallbladder contraction.

q: Where are most nutrients absorbed?
e: The small intestine's villi and microvilli give it a huge surface area. The large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.

q: Which cells produce antibodies?
a: Plasma cells, which develop from B cells
e: B cells activated by antigen (often with T-helper help) become plasma cells that secrete antibodies, or memory B cells.

q: Cytotoxic (CD8⁺) T cells recognize antigens presented on:
e: Nearly all nucleated cells show internal peptides on MHC I, so CD8⁺ T cells can find infected or cancerous cells. MHC II, found on antigen-presenting cells, is read by CD4⁺ helper T cells.

q: Which is part of the innate immune system?
e: Innate defenses respond quickly and nonspecifically, and include skin, macrophages, neutrophils, NK cells and complement. B and T cells are adaptive.

q: In skeletal muscle, calcium triggers contraction by binding to:
a: Troponin, which moves tropomyosin off myosin-binding sites on actin
w: Myosin heads, which then attach directly to binding sites on actin
Tropomyosin, which is cut and released from the actin filament
Actin, which then hydrolyzes ATP to pull itself along the myosin
e: With the binding sites exposed, myosin heads form cross-bridges and pull actin filaments toward the center of the sarcomere.

q: During skeletal muscle contraction, which part of the sarcomere stays the same length?
e: The A band is the length of the thick myosin filaments, which don't shorten. The H zone, I band and sarcomere all shorten as filaments slide.

q: In muscle contraction, ATP binding to the myosin head is needed to:
w: Pump sodium into the muscle cell
e: Without ATP, myosin stays locked to actin. That's why muscles stiffen in rigor mortis.

q: Which cells break down bone matrix and release calcium into the blood?
e: Osteoclasts resorb bone. Osteoblasts build new bone and become osteocytes once surrounded by matrix.

q: The LH surge in the middle of the menstrual cycle directly triggers:
e: Rising estrogen from the developing follicle switches to positive feedback and causes an LH surge. The leftover follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone.

q: Sperm mature and gain motility in the:
e: Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, then mature in the epididymis.

q: When body temperature rises, the skin helps cool the body by:
a: Dilating blood vessels near the surface and producing sweat
w: Constricting blood vessels and making the hairs stand up
Reducing blood flow to the skin
e: Vasodilation brings warm blood to the surface to lose heat, and evaporating sweat carries heat away.
